questions.stem: A 25-person firm just won two school projects. Its production workload will be about 30% above current capacity for the next four months, then drop back to normal. Cash reserves are modest. Which staffing approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Hire four permanent production staff immediately.
options.explanation: Permanent hires for a four-month peak leave the firm over-staffed and paying salaries and benefits once the workload falls. That's a poor fit with modest reserves.

options.text: Use a combination of short-term contract staff and limited, planned overtime.
options.explanation: Correct. Contract staff and limited overtime add capacity only for as long as the peak lasts, so the firm avoids long-term salary commitments and doesn't overwork the team for months.

options.text: Decline one of the school projects to stay within current capacity.
options.explanation: Turning away profitable, strategic work is a last resort when flexible capacity is readily available.

options.text: Require all staff to work 30% overtime for the four months.
options.explanation: Sustained heavy overtime costs a premium for non-exempt staff and risks burnout, errors and turnover. It's not a sound plan for four months.

questions.explanation: Match the type of resource to how long the need lasts: flex resources for a temporary peak, permanent hires for lasting growth.

questions.stem: A firm wants to expand from office work into healthcare projects. Which action best positions it to deliver these projects competently?

options.text: Buy healthcare-specific planning software and market the new service right away.
options.explanation: Tools without experienced people don't create competence. Marketing a service the firm can't yet deliver also raises ethical concerns about representing qualifications.

options.text: Hire or partner with experienced healthcare architects, and train existing staff on the relevant guidelines and regulations.
options.explanation: Correct. Bringing in experienced people (by hiring, joint venture or consultant) and training current staff builds real capability in a highly regulated building type.

options.text: Assign the firm's most senior office-building designer to lead the first healthcare project alone.
options.explanation: Seniority in another building type isn't healthcare expertise. One person working alone is a key-person and quality risk.

options.text: Lower fees on the first healthcare project to win it, and learn on the job.
options.explanation: Low fees don't build competence and leave less money for the extra effort a new building type demands. Learning on the job alone risks a standard-of-care failure.

questions.explanation: Moving into a new practice area takes people, knowledge and tools together. The ARE favors the answer that protects quality and the public.

questions.stem: A principal is evaluating a firm-wide switch to a new BIM platform. Which costs belong in a total-cost-of-ownership analysis?

options.text: Staff training time and course fees
options.explanation: Correct. Training is often a large share of the cost of a technology change.

options.text: Reduced productivity on active projects during the learning curve
options.explanation: Correct. Lost productivity while staff learn the new tool is a real cost and affects project fees.

options.text: Annual subscription or maintenance fees
options.explanation: Correct. Recurring software costs are part of owning the platform over time.

options.text: The construction cost of projects that will be designed with the software
options.explanation: Construction cost belongs to the client's project budget, not the firm's cost of owning a tool.

options.text: The consultants' fees on current projects
options.explanation: Consultant fees are project pass-through costs. They don't depend on the firm's software choice.

options.text: The owner's contingency for future projects
options.explanation: The owner's contingency is part of the client's budget and has nothing to do with the firm's investment decision.

questions.explanation: Total cost of ownership = acquisition + implementation + training + productivity loss + ongoing fees and support.

questions.stem: A firm is considering a $36,000 reality-capture system. It expects the system to save $15,000 a year in field-survey labor and bring in $9,000 a year in added profit from new renovation work. What is the simple payback period, in years?
Firm-wide utilization has climbed from 78% to 93% over two quarters. Overtime is rising and two project architects have resigned. What should management conclude first?

options.text: The firm is operating at peak efficiency and should keep current staffing.
options.explanation: Very high utilization combined with rising overtime and resignations signals overload, not healthy efficiency.

options.text: The firm needs added capacity, and staff workload should be rebalanced.
options.explanation: Correct. Sustained over-utilization, turnover and overtime together show the firm is under-staffed for its workload.

options.text: The firm should cut marketing time to raise utilization further.
options.explanation: Cutting non-billable activities like marketing and training gets the firm a little more billable time now but starves the future pipeline, and it makes burnout worse.

options.text: The firm should raise billing rates to reduce demand.
options.explanation: Raising rates may be appropriate for other reasons, but it doesn't address burnout and turnover now.

questions.explanation: Read utilization together with other indicators. Too high is as much a warning sign as too low.

questions.stem: Which practices make staff performance evaluations most useful and most defensible?

options.text: Evaluate against written expectations established in advance
options.explanation: Correct. Clear, pre-set expectations make reviews fair and measurable.

options.text: Document reviews and agreed development goals in writing
options.explanation: Correct. Written records support development planning and protect the firm if a personnel decision is challenged.

options.text: Hold reviews only when there is a performance problem
options.explanation: Problem-only reviews feel punitive and miss development opportunities. Regular reviews are better practice.

options.text: Base the review mainly on the employee's billable hours
options.explanation: Utilization is one data point. Quality, leadership and growth also matter.

options.text: Share peers' salaries so the employee can compare
options.explanation: Disclosing other employees' compensation raises confidentiality concerns and isn't part of a sound evaluation process.

options.text: Keep the evaluation verbal to encourage candor
options.explanation: Verbal-only reviews leave no record for development tracking or defense of employment actions.

questions.explanation: Good evaluations are regular, based on clear criteria, documented, and tied to development.

questions.stem: A small firm relies on one senior technical architect for all specifications and code reviews. Which resource strategy most directly reduces the firm's risk?

options.text: Give the architect a retention bonus.
options.explanation: A bonus may delay a departure, but the firm still depends on one person.

options.text: Cross-train other staff and document the architect's procedures in office standards.
options.explanation: Correct. Cross-training and written procedures spread the knowledge, which directly reduces key-person risk.

options.text: Outsource all specification writing permanently.
options.explanation: Outsourcing moves the dependence to an outside party and may lower quality-control oversight. It doesn't spread the knowledge inside the firm.

options.text: Buy key-person life insurance on the architect.
options.explanation: Insurance pays money if the person dies. It doesn't keep the knowledge in the firm or cover a resignation.

questions.explanation: Key-person risk is best handled by spreading knowledge: cross-training, written standards, and succession planning.

questions.stem: A firm has six projects moving from construction documents into construction over the next quarter. Which staffing adjustment is most appropriate?

options.text: Reassign staff with field and contract-administration experience to the projects entering construction.
options.explanation: Correct. Construction-phase services call for people who can review submittals, answer RFIs and observe the work.

options.text: Keep the original design teams on all projects at full staffing.
options.explanation: Construction administration usually needs fewer hours than CDs, and different skills. Full design teams would overspend the fee.

options.text: Hire additional designers to handle submittals.
options.explanation: Submittal review is a technical and contract-administration task, not a design task.

options.text: Assign construction administration to the most junior staff to save fee.
options.explanation: CA involves contractual judgment and liability exposure. Junior staff need supervision, not sole responsibility.

questions.explanation: Staffing should change with each project phase, matching both the skills required and the fee available.

questions.stem: A firm's strategic plan calls for offering energy-performance and sustainability consulting within two years. Which investments best support that goal?

options.text: Energy-modeling software with training for a core group of staff
options.explanation: Correct. A tool plus trained people gives the firm a deliverable capability for the new service.

options.text: Funding staff to earn relevant sustainability credentials and continuing education
options.explanation: Correct. Credentials and education build expertise and credibility in the new market.

options.text: Upgrading the office's furniture
options.explanation: Office comfort may matter, but it doesn't advance the new service line.

options.text: Larger-format plotters
options.explanation: Printing capacity has nothing to do with energy-performance services.

options.text: Hiring a second receptionist
options.explanation: Administrative staffing doesn't build technical sustainability capability.

options.text: Moving to a larger office before any sustainability projects are signed
options.explanation: Adding overhead ahead of revenue increases risk without building the required skills.

questions.explanation: Capital spending should map to strategic goals. Here that means people and tools that deliver the new service.

questions.stem: A firm can lease or buy a set of high-end workstations. It has strong profits but tight cash, because several large clients pay slowly. Which choice is generally most appropriate?

options.text: Buy the workstations outright to minimize lifetime cost.
options.explanation: Buying may cost less over the equipment's life, but it uses scarce cash the firm needs while receivables are slow.

options.text: Lease the workstations to preserve working capital.
options.explanation: Correct. When cash is tight, leasing spreads the cost over time and keeps cash available for payroll and operations.

options.text: Delay the purchase until profits increase.
options.explanation: Profits are already strong. The constraint is cash, not profitability, so waiting for more profit misreads the problem.

options.text: Finance the purchase by delaying payments to consultants.
options.explanation: Delaying consultant payments harms relationships and may breach agreements. It isn't a legitimate financing strategy.

questions.explanation: Profit and cash are different. Here a cash constraint, not a profit problem, drives the decision.

flashcards.back: Contracted work not yet earned. Compare it with staff capacity to forecast staffing needs.
Chargeable (billable) hours ÷ total hours. Too high signals overload; too low signals idle capacity.

flashcards.front: Best response to a short-term workload peak
flashcards.back: Flexible capacity: contract staff, limited overtime, or outsourcing a discrete task, not permanent hires.

flashcards.front: Best response to sustained growth or a new service line
flashcards.back: Permanent hires (or partners) with the right skills, supported by training.

flashcards.front: Total cost of ownership for technology
flashcards.back: Purchase or subscription + implementation + training + productivity loss while learning + ongoing support and upgrades.
Investment ÷ annual net benefit (savings + added profit).

flashcards.front: Lease vs. buy: when to lease
flashcards.back: When cash is tight or the technology turns over quickly. Leasing keeps working capital in the firm and makes upgrades easier.
Cross-training, written procedures and office standards, and succession planning.

flashcards.front: What a defensible staff evaluation needs
flashcards.back: Regular schedule, pre-set written expectations, documentation, and development goals.

flashcards.front: How staffing changes from CDs to construction
flashcards.back: Fewer hours, and shift to people with field, submittal and contract-administration skills.

flashcards.front: Three ingredients for entering a new practice area
flashcards.back: Experienced people (hire or partner), training or credentials, and the right tools, together.

flashcards.front: Why very high utilization is a warning sign
flashcards.back: No time left for marketing, training or QC; predicts overtime, burnout and turnover.
